head: 'Finchley' probably means the clearing where finches live.
text: It ends in Old English leah, a clearing in a wood. On the station stands a statue of an archer by Eric Aumonier, aiming his arrow towards central London.

head: 'Ham' means dry land in a river bend or between rivers.
text: The land here lies between the Thames, the Lea and the Roding. It was recorded about a century before the Normans as Hamme, and was split into East Ham and West Ham in the 12th century.

head: Named after the East India Docks, built in 1806 for the East India Company.
text: The company's big ships traded with India and China. The docks have been filled in, but parts of the old dock walls survive.

head: 'Putney' means the landing place of a man called Putta.
text: The Domesday Book of 1086 records it as Putelei. The landing place was on the Thames, where Putney Bridge is today.

head: 'Eastcote' means the cottage or cottages to the east.
text: They lay east of Ruislip; Ascot, near Windsor, has the same origin. The walled garden and dovecote of Eastcote House survive, although the house itself was demolished in the 1960s.

head: 'Edgware' probably means the fishing pool of a Saxon called Ecgi.
text: A 'wer' or weir was a pool or dam for catching fish. The Northern line reached Edgware in 1924 and was planned to go further, but the extension was never finished.

head: Named after the road to Edgware, which follows the Roman Watling Street.
text: Edgware probably means the fishing pool of a Saxon called Ecgi. The road runs dead straight to the north-west, as Roman roads do.

head: 'Edmonton' means the farm of a man called Ēadhelm.
text: It is in the Domesday Book of 1086 as Adelmetone. The essayist Charles Lamb lived in Edmonton in his last years and is buried in the churchyard.

head: Most likely named after a coaching inn called the Elephant and Castle.
text: A popular story says the name comes from 'Infanta de Castile', a Spanish princess, but historians doubt it. An elephant carrying a castle was a common sign, used for example by the Cutlers' Company.

head: The name was chosen in the 1930s for a new garden estate.
text: The estate was built on farmland between Hornchurch and Rainham, and the station opened in 1935 to serve it.

head: Named after Elverson Road, the street beside the station.
text: The origin of the street's name is not recorded. The station opened in 1999 on the DLR extension to Lewisham.

head: Named after the Victoria Embankment, built along the Thames in the 1860s.
text: Joseph Bazalgette built it to carry new sewers and the District Railway, and to create a riverside road. The station had many names with 'Charing Cross' in them before it became Embankment in 1976.

head: Named after an estate laid out from 1895 by the developer William Carter.
text: The name is said to come from Carter's son, Emerson. The station opened in 1909 to serve the new houses.

head: 'Enfield' means the open land of a man called Ēana, or where lambs were reared.
text: It comes from Old English feld, open country. In 1967 the world's first cash machine was installed at a bank in Enfield.

head: 'Epping' probably means the people of the upland.
text: It is in the Domesday Book of 1086 as Eppinges. The great forest nearby takes its name from the town, not the other way round.

head: Named after Euston Hall in Suffolk, home of the Dukes of Grafton.
text: The dukes owned the land here, and Euston Road and Euston Square took the name of their country house. The Suffolk village of Euston probably means the farm of a man called Efe.

head: Named after Euston Square, the garden square near the main line station.
text: The name comes from Euston Hall in Suffolk, home of the Dukes of Grafton, who owned the land. The station opened in 1863 as Gower Street and was renamed in 1909.

head: Named after the Fairlop Oak, a giant tree in Hainault Forest.
text: From the early 18th century a fair was held every summer under the oak, started by a local man, Daniel Day. The tree was damaged by fire and blew down in the early 19th century.

head: Named after Nicholas and William de Faringdon, aldermen of the City.
text: They owned land here in the 13th century, and their name passed to a City ward, a street and the station. Farringdon was one of the first stations of the world's first underground railway, opened in 1863.

head: 'Finchley' probably means the clearing where finches live.
text: The station opened on a railway line in 1867 and was called Finchley (Church End) until 1940, when it became Finchley Central.

head: Named after the road to Finchley, built in the 1820s as a turnpike.
text: Finchley probably means the clearing where finches live. The new road avoided the steep hills of Hampstead further east.

head: 'Frognal' means the nook where frogs live.
text: It comes from Old English frogga, frog, and healh, a nook. Finchley Road was built in the 1820s as a new road to Finchley.

head: Named after a park opened in 1869, though it is not in Finsbury.
text: The park was planned for the people of the old borough of Finsbury, further south. 'Finsbury' probably means the manor of a man called Finn.

head: Named after a gate that kept animals from straying out of Epping Forest.
text: Cattle grazing in the forest could wander onto the main road to Romford, so a gate was put across it. It was removed in the 19th century, but the name stayed.

head: Named after the Great North Wood, which once covered the hill.
text: The wood stretched across the hills of south London. Forest Hill is home to the Horniman Museum.

head: 'Fulham' means the riverside land of a man called Fulla.
text: It was recorded as Fulanham around 700. The station opened in 1880 as Walham Green, after the local village green, and was renamed Fulham Broadway in 1952.

head: Named after a stretch of the Thames, recalling the Galyon family.
text: The family owned property by the river in the 14th century. Rudyard Kipling mentions Gallions in his 1890 novel The Light that Failed.

head: Probably named after the le Gant family, stewards of Barking Abbey's lands.
text: The family is recorded here from the 13th century. The station, opened in 1947, has a long vaulted hall between the platforms, inspired by the Moscow Metro.

head: Named after Gidea Hall, a mansion first recorded in the 13th century.
text: The name may mean 'the giddy or foolish hall', perhaps for an odd-looking building. In 1910–11 a garden suburb was built here, with a competition for the best-designed houses.

head: Named after Maria, Duchess of Gloucester, who built a house here in 1805.
text: Before that the road was called Hog Moore Lane. The station opened in 1868 as Brompton (Gloucester Road).

head: Named after the Godyere family, who held land here in the 14th century.
text: The green was open land next to their property. The village grew quickly after the Underground arrived in 1907.

head: Probably named after John Goldhawk, a landowner in the 15th century.
text: He held a large amount of land in the area, then part of the parish of Fulham. The station opened in 1914.

head: Named after John Goodge, who developed the land from 1746.
text: Before the houses were built it was a meadow called Crab Tree Field. The station opened in 1907 as Tottenham Court Road and was renamed Goodge Street a year later.

head: Probably named after John Godemay, a 14th-century landowner.
text: His family's name survived as the name of a farm. The station opened in 1901, and the houses around it followed.

head: Named after an oak tree where the gospel was read at the parish boundary.
text: When people walked the boundary of the parish each year, 'beating the bounds', they stopped under the tree to read from the Bible. It marked the border between Hampstead and St Pancras.

head: A 'grange' was a farm with barns, often belonging to a monastery.
text: This one stood on a hill. The name has no link with the children's TV series Grange Hill.

head: Named after the street, which honours the Dukes of Portland.
text: The 2nd Duke of Portland owned the land from 1734. The station opened in 1863 as Portland Road.

head: Named after the park, renamed The Green Park in 1746.
text: It was first called Upper St James's Park. The new name probably described its open grassland with few trees and no flower beds. The station opened in 1906 as Dover Street.

head: 'Greenford' means the green ford.
text: The ford crossed the River Brent. In 1857 William Perkin opened a factory here to make mauve, the first synthetic dye.

head: 'Greenwich' means the green trading place or harbour.
text: It was first recorded in the early 10th century. Greenwich is home to the Royal Observatory and the prime meridian, the line of zero longitude that sets Greenwich Mean Time.

head: 'Gunnersbury' means the manor of a woman called Gunnhild.
text: Gunnhild is a Scandinavian name. A legend links it to a niece of King Canute, but there is no proof.

head: 'Hackney' means the island of a man called Haca.
text: The 'island' was dry raised ground in the marshes of the River Lea. It was recorded in 1198 as Hakeneia.

head: Named after Hackney Downs, an open common in Hackney.
text: 'Downs' means hill land. Hackney means the island of a man called Haca, a patch of dry ground in the marshes.

head: 'Wick' comes from Old English wīc, a farm or small settlement.
text: It was the part of Hackney beside the River Lea. Much of the London 2012 Olympic Park is next to it.

head: 'Haggerston' means the boundary stone of a man called Hærgod.
text: It is in the Domesday Book of 1086 as Hergotestane. The station opened in 2010 on the new East London line.

head: 'Hainault' probably means the wood of a religious community.
text: It was recorded in 1221 as Henehout, from Old English for a monastery wood, here belonging to Barking Abbey. The French-looking spelling came later, from a mistaken link with Philippa of Hainault, wife of Edward III.

head: 'Hammersmith' probably means a place with a hammer smithy, or forge.
text: It was first recorded in 1294. Another, less likely theory sees in it a landing place belonging to a man called Hammoder.

head: 'Hampstead' simply means homestead.
text: It comes from Old English hām-stede, like Berkhamsted and Wheathampstead. Hampstead station, opened in 1907, has the deepest platforms on the Underground.

head: Named after Hampstead Heath, one of London's largest open spaces.
text: 'Hampstead' simply means homestead. The heath has bathing ponds and, on Parliament Hill, one of the best views over London.

head: 'Hanger' means a wooded slope.
text: It comes from Old English hangra, a wood on a steep hillside. The same word gives Hanger Hill nearby.

head: 'Hanwell' probably means the spring where cockerels or wild birds gather.
text: It was recorded in 959 as Hanewelle. Just west of the station is the Wharncliffe Viaduct, built by Isambard Kingdom Brunel for the Great Western Railway and opened in 1838.

head: 'Harlesden' means the farm of a man called Heoruwulf.
text: It is recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086 as Herulvestune, with -tune meaning a farm. Bakerloo trains have called here since 1917.

head: Named after King Harold, who held land here before 1066.
text: Harold II was killed at the Battle of Hastings in 1066. His name survived in the wood, recorded in the 13th century as Horoldeswode.
